title: Transfer to Korea, the Seventh Infantry Division Band and Korean life
summary: A levy sends him to Korea instead of Saigon; he plays with saxophonist Carter Jefferson and shares Charlie Parker records.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: I showed you how I got in and all this and that. So now we’re over on Staten Island with the New York Army Band and a levy comes down from Washington. Man, I was the drummer with the stage band. And everybody figured well D’Imperio’s never going to get transferred out of here because there’s nobody to replace him. And our First Sergeant’s name was Joe College, or Howard Joe College, we called him J.C. And he said these — J.C.’s man they’re just not going to be able to take him away, you know. Well the Army doesn’t quite work that way. And he called me up in latrine, and he said, “Danny, a levy’s come down from Washington and you’re being transferred someplace in the Orient. We don’t know where yet, but we’re going to call Sergeant Shipp,” who had already been transferred over there — S-H-I-P-P, “and try to get you in the Saigon band.” I said, oh gee, this is wonderful. Okay, now I’m heading from like New York City right to Saigon, or worse you know. Because there were several division bands. See there was headquarter bands and there were division bands. Well anyway, the way it turned out was my orders were for Korea. So I mean that was a blessing unto itself you know. I mean it’s not going to be Vietnam, it’s going to be Korea. So now I get to what I thought was going to be the Eighth Army Headquarters Band in Seoul. So I get off my duffle bag and go in there, I’m coming in and, “oh you’re from the New York Army Band and I see your rating was 97” and all this and that, I guess it was a recommendation. But the Seventh Infantry Division Band needs a drummer. And I said oh here we go. So now I head up towards the DMZ and I’m in the Seventh Infantry Division Band. Now in that © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

band was Carter Jefferson, the tenor player who was with Woody Shaw for years, with the Jazz Messengers, you know, later on. But he didn’t know anything about — he had been with Little Richard and Jackie Wilson, bands like that. He was a black saxophone player from Washington. And I brought a bunch of tapes of Charlie Parker and this and that, which then I bought an Ampex reel to reel and we used to just sit and listen to that stuff and that’s sort of the way he developed into a fine jazz player. He’s since gone to his reward. But we were up there and we ravaged that country pretty good. In fact I delivered two twin sons up there. One of them is a principal bassist now with the Washington Opera, and the other one is a physicist in Brookhaven Lab. But we ravaged the hell out of Korea.
Well I mean it was a smorgasbord of females, and there was more drugs than we could absorb.
And the Korean War was over.
No, no, this was during the Vietnam era.
So America’s presence was like post-war.
